elements.text: Inadequate consideration of human factors limitations in United Airlines' engine overhaul inspection and quality control procedures
Failure to detect a fatigue crack originating from a previously undetected metallurgical defect in the stage 1 fan disk
Metallurgical defect located in a critical area of the stage 1 fan disk manufactured by General Electric Aircraft Engines
Catastrophic disintegration of the fan disk
Liberation of debris with energy levels exceeding the protection provided by the DC-10's hydraulic system design features
Weather was not a factor in this accident
Air Traffic Control services were supportive and not a factor in the accident
Uncontained failure of the No. 2 engine stage 1 fan rotor disk assembly
No. 2 engine fragments severed the No. 1 and No. 3 hydraulic system lines
Forces of the engine failure fractured the No. 2 hydraulic system
Rendering the airplane's three hydraulic-powered flight control systems inoperative
No alternative power sources for the flight control systems in wide-body design transport airplanes
Airplane was marginally flyable using asymmetrical thrust but a safe landing was virtually impossible
Cornstalks on the airfield adversely affected firefighting operations
Failure of the Kovatch P-18 water supply vehicle adversely affected firefighting operations
FAA has not adequately addressed the issue of infant occupant protection
Separation of the titanium alloy stage 1 fan rotor disk was the result of a fatigue crack
Fatigue crack initiated from a type 1 hard alpha metallurgical defect on the surface of the disk bore
Hard alpha metallurgical defect formed during manufacture of the ingot from which the disk was forged
Hard alpha metallurgical defect was not detected by ultrasonic and macroetch inspections performed by General Electric Aircraft Engines during manufacturing
Metallurgical flaw would have been apparent if the part had been macroetch inspected in its final part shape
Cavity associated with the hard alpha metallurgical defect was created during final machining and/or shot peening at GEAE
Hard alpha defect area cracked with the application of stress during initial exposures to full thrust engine power conditions
Crack grew until it entered material unaffected by the hard alpha defect
General Electric Aircraft Engines material and production records for the failed disk were incomplete
Two S/N HPO 00385 disks existed, with one rejected for ultrasonic indication held by an outside laboratory
Two S/N MPO 00385 disks were not switched at the manufacturing facility
General Electric Aircraft Engines disk manufacturing records and audit system did not assure accurate traceability of turbine engine rotating components
United Airlines fan disk maintenance records indicated maintenance was in accordance with approved programs
A detectable fatigue crack about 0.5 inch long existed at the time of the most recent United Airlines inspection in April 1988 but was not detected
Discoloration on the surface of the fatigue crack was created during the FPI process performed by UAL
Inspection parameters established in United Airlines and GEAE procedures are adequate to identify unserviceable rotating parts if properly followed
